### D438. The verified address reaches the API only sealed by the email issuer; the vault keeps the blob, the popup reads it through the API
- Date 2026-11-06 · Status: decided while building, **confirmed by the user 2026-11-09** · Built: `packages/email/src/sealed.ts`, the issuer's
  `handlers.ts` (google-match, google-record, verify), `packages/web/src/vault/vault.ts`, `apps/api/src/identity/email.ts`
- Decision: the identity token spec's sealed email (D127, its AAD already pinned by core's vectors): the issuer seals
  the address it verified (Google's userinfo address, lowercased; or the normalized login address) under a new
  `IDENTITY_SEAL_KEY` shared with the API, bound to the app, the session key and the session's expiry, in every
  successful google-match and google-record and in a `verify` that mints a `session` token, whatever the app's
  setting. The vault keeps the blob with the session (memory and its IndexedDB record) and sends it with each mint and
  consent call; it can't open it. The sheet in the auth popup gets the address from `POST
  /v1/identity/email-consent/preview` (`Origin: AUTH_ORIGIN` only) with a single-use `preview` session proof the vault
  made, so the address never reaches the vault frame or the partner page.
- Why: the API can't verify an address any other way (it has no issuer binding, and the issuer's directory is staff
  only, D275); sealing always (rather than only for apps with sharing on) needs no issuer read of the API's new column,
  so no deploy order can break email logins.
- Rejected: the API reading the issuer's directory (breaks D275's "no other Worker binds the issuer"); the popup
  asserting the address (anyone could share a false address as `email_verified: true`); the API calling Google's
  tokeninfo itself (no answer for email logins, and the access token is gone after login).

### D439. One consent table keyed by app, User ID and an address MAC under a new EMAIL_CONSENT_KEY; email search is an exact MAC lookup
- Date 2026-11-06 · Status: decided while building, **confirmed by the user 2026-11-09** · Built: `apps/api/migrations/0014_email_sharing.sql`,
  `apps/api/src/identity/email.ts`, `apps/api/src/directory/read.ts`
- Decision: hot-D1 `email_consents (app_id, user_sub, email_mac, state, email, scope_id, decided_at)`, PK app × User ID
  (`u1_…`) × `HMAC-SHA256(EMAIL_CONSENT_KEY, "hana-id/email-consent/v1" ‖ 0x00 ‖ lowercase address)`; `email` (the
  dashboard's copy) is set exactly while the row is `granted`. `EMAIL_CONSENT_KEY` is a new API-only secret (no doc gives
  `IDENTITY_SUB_KEY` or `USER_ID_KEY` that purpose), generated with `IDENTITY_SEAL_KEY` by `identity-key <env>
  email-keys`. A partner's email search is a full address only, matched by its MAC among the org's `granted` rows. A
  revoke covers every address of the app × account. Rows go with `uid-erase` and 30 days after the app's deletion.
- Why: a declined address must be remembered without being kept; an exact MAC match can't be used to probe prefixes
  or unshared addresses (D315).
- Trade-offs: rotating `EMAIL_CONSENT_KEY` would ask every user again (it is never rotated in normal operation).

### D440. The consent endpoints take the identity token's session proof over their own payload, and check the share and session as a mint does
- Date 2026-11-06 · Status: decided while building, **confirmed by the user 2026-11-09** · Built: `apps/api/src/identity/email.ts`,
  `packages/core/src/identity.ts` `emailConsentPayload` (vectors in `identity-v1.json`)
- Decision: `POST /v1/identity/email-consent/state`, `/v1/identity/email-consent`, `/revoke` (vault origin) and
  `/preview` (auth origin); each a single-use session proof (±60 s, the mint's marker) over `"email-consent" ‖
  borsh(action) ‖ borsh(parent_origin) ‖ sha256(sealed_email or "")`; the share ('session' mode) and the on-chain
  session as the mint checks them; the account from the session's path. A decision or a preview is refused while the
  setting is `off` (`409 identity_email_off`); a revoke always works, also while the contract is paused. Without the
  keys every endpoint answers `503 email_sharing_unavailable`.
- Why: the decision binds to the account through the session, never through a page's word (the identity token spec's
  rule), and reuses checks already reviewed.

### D441. Tokens carry the session's own address when it is shared; a session without a readable seal gets the latest shared one
- Date 2026-11-06 · Status: decided while building, **confirmed by the user 2026-11-09** · Built: `apps/api/src/identity/email.ts` `mintEmail`
- Decision: setting `off` → `emailStatus: 'off'`. A seal that opens → its own consent decides (`included` with that
  address, `declined`, `not_asked`). No seal, or one that can't be opened (the issuer was unreachable at login, a key
  rotated past its overlap) → the account's most recently shared address for the app (`included`), else `missing` /
  `invalid`. A D1 or key failure gives no email, never a failed mint.
- Why: a linked second address isn't shared until asked (D411 point 5), but a session that simply lacks a blob
  shouldn't lose an address the user did share.

### D442. The sheet is its own auth page; at login the popup ends on it; the approval popup's account line and the sheet revoke
- Date 2026-11-06 · Status: decided while building, **confirmed by the user 2026-11-09** · Built: `packages/web/src/auth/share-page.ts`,
  `share-handoff.ts`, `vault/email-share.ts`, `approve-page.ts`
- Decision: `/share-email` (CSP `connect-src` the API only). `at_login`: auth-params carry `emailShare`, and the login
  popup, instead of closing at the end (the callback after its relay, the email step on the vault's `done`), goes to
  `/share-email?from=login`; the vault, after the key passed its check and before it answers the login, reads the state
  and shows the sheet there when it is `not_asked`, else tells the window to close; for a Google record-only login it
  awaits google-record (30 s at most) for the blob. A closed popup, no hello within 20 s, or any failure: the login
  finishes, asked again next time. `requestEmailSharing()`: the SDK opens `/share-email?from=partner&v=…` in the click
  (the launcher when blocked); an address already shared shows "Stop sharing" / "Done". The approval popup's account
  line shows "Email shared with {App} · Stop sharing" while the vault's last known state is `granted`. "Share email" is
  the approval popup's guarded button (D36); the D42 caveat is shown for an app on its own Google client.
- Why: the login state machine stays as it was (one flag and two close points); the sheet works the same in both
  places; D411 point 6 names the popup's account view, and the approval popup's account line is its only one (D395).
- Trade-off: an app whose signing is all auto-approved shows users no approval popup, so its only revoke path until
  Hana Home is the sheet the partner opens.
- Amended 2026-11-09 (the user): an app that has an auto-approve policy and email sharing on must offer its users a
  visible control that calls `requestEmailSharing()`, so every user can stop sharing. It is a requirement in
  `docs/integration.md`, not technically enforced; Hana Home's revoke replaces it.

### D443. SDK 0.3.0: requestEmailSharing() resolves granted, declined or dismissed; emailSharingChanged; useEmailSharing
- Date 2026-11-06 · Status: decided while building, **confirmed by the user 2026-11-09** · Built: `packages/web/src/client/client.ts`,
  `packages/react/src/email-sharing.ts`, `packages/core/src/protocol.ts`; all four packages at 0.3.0
- Decision: `hana.requestEmailSharing(): Promise<'granted' | 'declined' | 'dismissed'>` (`dismissed`: the window
  closed, nothing recorded); errors `email_sharing_unavailable` (`data.reason` `off`, `no_address`, `unavailable`) and
  4100 when logged out. The vault sends `emailSharingChanged {state}` only to an SDK of `EMAIL_SHARING_SDK_MIN` (0.3.0)
  or later (D393's gate) and drops its cached identity token silently (not `identityTokenChanged(null)`, which means
  logged out). React: `useEmailSharing()` → `{request, state, error}`.
- Why: the spec's `'granted' | 'declined'` can't tell a closed window from "Not now"; a closed window must record
  nothing (never mandatory, D411 point 7).

### D436. The mainnet demo values with CoinGecko's live prices, in a band ending at the fixed table
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **asked for by the user 2026-11-09**; the mechanics below confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built:
  `feat/mainnet-demo-live-prices`, not merged, not deployed · Amends D429's price table. Closes the sample's FRICTION 23–28.
- The problem: with D429's fixed table (ETH $8,000, XLM $1.00, USDC $1.05, EURC $1.35) the $9.99 cap really allowed
  about $2.68 of ETH or $1.48 of XLM at the market of 2026-11-09, and the page couldn't see the prices, so its own
  "Max" was refused.
- Decision (the user's): live prices from CoinGecko, with the user's Pro key, falling back to non-Pro if there's no key
  or the key isn't Pro.
  1. **The API Worker fetches, never the vault or the browser.** Worker secret `COINGECKO_API_KEY`, optional. Only for
     `GET /v1/app` of an app with the demo on, in a dev env on testnet (`mainnetDemoOn`); a production manifest never
     reaches it.
  2. **Source order per refresh**: key → Pro API with `x-cg-pro-api-key`; if the key is refused → the public host with
     it as `x-cg-demo-api-key`; then, or without a key → the public host with no key; then the fixed table. The key is
     only ever in its header. CoinGecko's 400/401/403 and its codes 10002/10010/10011 (checked against its error
     reference and a live call on 2026-11-09: an invalid key answers `401` with `error_code: 10002`) mean "refused";
     anything else from Pro skips the Demo attempt (a real Pro key isn't valid on the public host).
  3. **Cache** 5 minutes, in the Cache API and in the isolate (below), up to 15 minutes old while a background refresh
     runs (`waitUntil`). A live price older than 15 minutes isn't used.
  4. **The band**: price used = live × 1.05, rounded up to the micro in exact decimal arithmetic, clamped to a floor (ETH
     $1,000, XLM $0.07, USDC $0.95, EURC $1.00) and a ceiling (the fixed table), per asset; out of range is clamped and
     logged (warning, no value or key); an asset missing, malformed or older than 15 minutes is the fixed price for
     that asset. The fixed table's expiry still refuses (`mainnet_demo_prices_stale`) a request that depends on a fixed
     price past 2026-12-21; live prices don't depend on that date.
  5. **The vault stays the decider**: it receives the book in `GET /v1/app`'s `mainnetDemoPrices`, re-validates it
     strictly against the same constants (`parseMainnetDemoPrices`, `@hana-id/core/mainnet-demo-prices`) and values each
     request with it; the approval popup does the same with the book the vault sends it, for its value and balance lines.
  6. **The page sees the prices in force**: `hana.mainnetDemo.prices` (per asset, source, time) and `mainnetDemoChanged`.
- To confirm (details chosen while building):
  - **Isolate memo as well as the Cache API.** Cloudflare documents the Cache API for custom domains; on `workers.dev`
    (sandbox-dev's API) it is reported to do nothing. So the isolate's copy is what bounds the calls there, and the
    Cache API adds a colo-wide bound where it does work. Calls are at most one refresh per isolate per 5 minutes while
    healthy; a failing CoinGecko is asked at most once per isolate per 60 s (`REFRESH_GATE_MS`). No new cron, D1 row or
    paid feature (D417).
  - **Cold path**: with no live price at all, a request waits at most 1.2 s (`COLD_WAIT_MS`) for the refresh (each attempt
    2.5 s, in the background under `waitUntil`), then answers the fixed table. One in 15 minutes per isolate pays it.
  - **Redirects aren't followed** (`redirect: 'manual'`; Workers has no `'error'` mode), so the key header can't be
    carried to another host.
  - **Per-asset source and the expiry** when an answer is partial: only assets actually used by the request can make it
    `prices_stale`; a book entirely on the table refuses first, as before.
  - **The book's `atMs` is the oldest live price's own CoinGecko time** (`last_updated_at`, which every attempt asks for
    and an asset without one is treated as malformed), so the 15-minute rule covers CoinGecko's age too.
  - **A separate `mainnetDemoPrices` port event** (sent before `mainnetDemo` when it first turns on, and on each
    change), not a new field on `mainnetDemo`: that event's validator takes exact keys, so a new field would make an
    SDK 0.2.0 drop the whole state. An older SDK drops the new event and keeps working. `mainnetDemo.prices` is null
    with a vault that predates it.
  - **The vault re-reads `GET /v1/app` every 5 minutes while the demo is on** (every minute while only the table could
    be had), so `hana.mainnetDemo.prices` follows the market without a sign request; a demo build only.
  - **The popup's book isn't part of the approval digest.** It only changes what the popup shows; the vault decides with
    the same book, and a vault compromised enough to lie here can sign without it anyway.
  - **`hana.mainnetDemoKnown` / `useMainnetDemo()`'s `known`** is true once `ready` resolved (the vault announces before
    `ready`), the answer to FRICTION 27; the React hook gives `{ demo, known }`.
  - The shipped `.d.ts` comments were cleared of decision numbers and internal paths, and `pack:check` now fails on any
    new one (`typeCommentProblems`); SDK versions bumped to 0.2.1 (lockstep, D72).
- Why this and not alternatives: (a) Pyth or another on-chain feed: the vault doesn't read an oracle, and Base/Stellar
  feeds would add RPC trust for no gain over a band. (b) Fetching in the vault or the browser: exposes a key and adds a
  CSP origin. (c) Removing the fixed table: it is what fails closed. (d) D1 as the cache store, a globally consistent
  bound: writes and a migration for a dev-only demo; revisit if the isolate bound proves too loose.
- Security: CoinGecko is now trusted within the band, no more (security.md "The mainnet demo"). Worst case: a lying feed
  drives ETH to its floor, so the cap passes 0.00999 ETH; at the market of 2026-11-09 ($2,144) that is about $21.42 for
  one transaction, and at most $79.92 if ETH were at the band's top. XLM the same way: 142.7 XLM, about $21.12 at the
  market, $142.71 at the band's top. USDC and EURC are bounded by their narrow bands ($11.04, $13.49). No per-day cap
  (the user's choice, D428), so the exposure is per signed transaction; every one is still an approval popup.
- Deploy order: the secret, then the API, then the vault and auth pages together (`deploy:pages`); the tarballs last. An
  older vault ignores the API's field; a newer vault without it uses the fixed table; a newer SDK with an older vault
  sees `prices: null`.
### D444. A partner turns email on per app in two steps: the app's setting, then the scope's email client on chain
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built on `feat/email-login-9`: `apps/console/src/email.ts`, `actions.ts`
  (`app.settings` `loginMethods`), `writes.ts` (`GET …/email`, `off` `what: 'email'`), `web/src/pages/app/EmailLogin.tsx`;
  `apps/api/src/changes/settings.ts`, `views.ts`; console-core `updateSettingsInput`, `turnOffInput`, `AppDetail.settings.loginMethods`,
  `AppSummary.emailOn`
- Decision: email login is per app (`apps.login_methods`) and needs the scope's client `("email", "email:<scope>")` on chain.
  Step 1: an owner turns the app's setting on with a fresh sign-in (`app.settings`, `loginMethods: 'google,email'`; the
  API's `updateSettings`; only with an email issuer bound). Step 2: an on-chain owner proposes `AddClient` (D447, timelocked);
  once it unlocks anyone executes it from the page or the Scope page. Email starts only when both hold; the issuer and `/v1/app`
  already require both. Turning off is a kill switch (`turnOff` `what: 'email'`: a second click, no sign-in, a frozen org
  too), immediate, for that app only. Removing the scope's client is a separate `remove_client` (immediate, fresh sign-in),
  offered only with no other app of the scope using email (the client is per scope).
- Why two steps: the client proof exists only once an active app of the scope has email on (the issuer's check, tokens
  review L6), so the setting goes first; a fresh sign-in can't commit to the settings digest and the owner-action digest at once.
- To confirm: "guarded like an origin change" (D32) is met by the fresh sign-in, the record in `app_changes`, and the chain's
  timelock on the client. A second app of a scope whose client already exists takes effect right after step 1, with no
  delay (that scope's users can already use email in another of its apps).
- Rejected: one fresh sign-in over both digests (the contract checks an owner-action nonce over its own args; a combined
  digest is a contract change); a 24 h D1 delay for the setting (the client's timelock is the delay that matters, and D1
  alone gives no access).
- Amended 2026-11-09 (branch `fix/batch-9-review`, batch 9's security review L3): the no-delay rule stands, and an out-of-band
  notice is added. Every `settings.changed` row with `loginMethods` gets a mail of its own to the alias and the org's security
  contacts: what changed, which app, and how to undo it (any owner, the app's Email login page, at once, no fresh sign-in). Both
  directions, and staff changes as well as a partner's, since the API writes the row. **The path:** the review asked for the origin
  change's `change_pending` path, but that is the guarded-change lifecycle: `guarded_changes.kind` is CHECK-limited to three kinds
  (a D1 table rebuild), and its ack starts a delay and issues a cancel token, neither of which applies to a change already in force.
  The notice instead rides the same 5-minute cron's `app_changes` feed, which already mailed these rows as a bare digest line: same
  sender, recipients as `change_pending` (alias and contacts), the run's call budget (D280, D380), a cursor that moves only past
  accepted sends. So it is at-least-once and after the fact. `src/feed.ts`, `email/messages.ts` `loginMethodsChanged`.

### D445. Link counts per app and day come from the contract's own events, seen as each relayed transaction settles
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built on `feat/email-login-9`: `apps/api/src/link-usage.ts`,
  `near/tx.ts` (`linkEventsFrom`), `relayer-key.ts`, `login.ts`, `handlers.ts`, `links.ts`; migration 0015 `link_usage`;
  `AdminRpc.linkStats`
- Decision: `link_usage` (app, UTC day) counts `identity_link_proposed`, `identity_linked`, `identity_link_activated`,
  `identity_link_cancelled`, `identity_unlinked` and the `auto` flag, parsed from the settled outcome's NEP-297 lines of
  receipts the signer executed; counted after the response on every session-pool relay (`/v1/login`, `/v1/sessions`,
  `/v1/derive`, `/v1/sessions/revoke`, `/v1/link*`, since a pending link can activate on any of them). Keys in those lines
  are never read out. Staff read it through `AdminRpc.linkStats` (a member actor is refused; counts only).
- Why: the spec's four counters and auto vs explicit are facts about the chain, and activation happens lazily on a later
  call. A transaction that fails counts nothing; a call direct to the contract (the partner's own relayer) isn't seen.
- Kept like `email_usage` (aggregate counts, deleted with the app).
- Rejected: an indexer over the contract's logs (a new cron, D417); counting at the request (activation isn't visible there).

### D446. Issuer counters per app and day (`email_daily`); five alert kinds counted and emailed from the issuer, at most once a day
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 (its provisional limits stay provisional, to tune on real traffic) (the numbers below) · Built on `feat/email-login-9`:
  `apps/email-issuer/src/daily.ts`, `handlers.ts`, `sendgrid.ts`, `webhook.ts`, `directory-rpc.ts` (`issuerStats`), migration 0004;
  `@hana-id/sendgrid` `customArgs`; `scripts/lib/admin-retention.ts`
- Decision: `email_daily (day, app_id, metric, count)` holds `sent`, `bounced`, `complained`, `refused:<limit>` and
  `alert:<event>[:code]`. `refused:*` stops counting at 1,000 per app, limit and day (the upsert writes nothing past it: an
  attacker can't burn D1 writes, D417). Bounces and complaints reach the right app by a SendGrid custom arg (`hana_app`,
  an app id, never an address). `DirectoryRpc.issuerStats` answers these and issuance per day/app/purpose (from
  `email_issuance`): counts only, so no staff audit row and no row budget. `retention:issuer` deletes `email_daily` past 24 months.
- Alerts: `send_budget_exhausted`, `email_budget`, `email_owner_pool`, `email_domain_cap`, `mailbox_guess_limit` are counted at
  every occurrence (the build plan's batch 9 list), and mailed to `SECURITY_ALIAS` from the issuer's own SendGrid at most once
  per kind, code and app a UTC day and at most 20 a day in all (limiter objects; no cron; `bypassSuppressions` as other alerts).
  Numbers provisional.
- Why: the issuer sees these at the moment they happen; the admin Worker's crons have no staff Access JWT to read the issuer
  with (D275) and no spare cron exists (5 of 5).
- Rejected: reading `DirectoryRpc` from a cron (a staff call without a person); an unbounded refusal counter.
- Amended 2026-11-09 (branch `fix/batch-9-review`, batch 9's security review L1, L2): **Alert mail:** at most once per kind, code, app
  and subject a UTC day (the subject is 12 characters of the mailbox's or domain's limiter key, never an address and never in a mail,
  log or metric name through this path), and at most 5 a day per kind instead of 20 in all, so tripping a limit on one's own mailbox
  or domain doesn't drop the alert for a real target and no kind starves another. Residual: five distinct subjects of one kind still
  use up that kind's day. **Bounded writes:** `alert:*` counters stop at 1,000 like `refused:*`. The webhook no longer writes one
  statement per event: Cloudflare's D1 limit is 50 queries per Worker invocation on the free plan (D417; `db.batch()` counts as one,
  https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/limits/, read 2026-11-09), so a 1000-event batch could fail after the 50th count and,
  with a complaint in it, answer 500 and be double-counted on retry. The suppressions, one count per (app, metric) and the dedupe keys
  are now one batch (migration 0005 `email_webhook_events`; SHA-256 of SendGrid's `sg_event_id`, which its docs give for deduplication,
  or of the event's fields without one), and a redelivery adds nothing. Written in that batch rather than through `countDaily`'s `n`,
  whose `waitUntil` write can't be atomic with the dedupe keys. A batch still counts one event per address, as before; keys are purged
  after 7 days by `retention:issuer` (SendGrid retries for up to 24 hours).

### D447. A partner's AddClient for email: the console gets the proof from the issuer over a service binding
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, **a product choice confirmed by the user 2026-11-09** (it softens the spec's "minted for staff only") ·
  Built on `feat/email-login-9`: `apps/email-issuer/src/console-rpc.ts`, `handlers.ts` (`mintPartnerClientProof`); console
  `actions.ts` (`AddEmailClient`, `remove_client` for the email aud); API `owner-actions.ts`, `validate.ts`; console gen `ISSUER`
- Decision: `ConsoleIssuerRpc` (entrypoint, no route, bound only by the console Worker) mints the same client proof as the staff
  route for the owner action the console is building: the scope registered, `action_nonce` current, an active app with email on,
  audited in `email_admin_audit` as `partner-console` (org, actor, request id), 20 per scope and UTC day. A proof binds one scope
  and action nonce and only an on-chain owner's token can use it. The API prechecks the email proof (JWS JSON, the published keys
  and on-chain signer policy, `aud`, `sub`, client-proof nonce) before relaying `propose_change`; a Google proof is refused.
  `remove_client` works for the email client, the last-client rule unchanged. The same entrypoint's `deliverability` gives an app's
  mail counts; the console calls it only after `getApp` confirmed the app is the org's.
- Why: partners enable email themselves (Q20); without this a Hana staff member must mint every partner's proof by hand, and
  "partner console: the email toggle" can't work.
- Rejected: keeping staff-only proofs (a manual step per partner); a public mint route.

### D448. The admin's Email issuer and Account links pages; the link-rate alert in the 15-minute cron
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 (the screens approved; its provisional limits stay provisional, to tune on real traffic) (5× median, floor 10, provisional, the spec's numbers plus a floor) ·
  Built on `feat/email-login-9`: `apps/admin/src/email-views.ts`, `link-alerts.ts`, `link-jumps.ts`, `near.ts`, `public/app.js`, gen

  whose links today are ≥ 5× its 7-day median and ≥ 10. The 15-minute cron reads `linkStats` once (one RPC of D380's budget, placed

## Hana Home: the build plan's decisions (branch `docs/hana-home-h0`), 2026-11-09

Settled by the user on the review of the Hana Home spec against `develop` (`docs/hana-home-build-plan.md`). None changes a
path, a key or derivation.

### D460. Turning off shared login waits the scope's delay and needs a remaining Google client
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09**; **reversed by the user the same day (D480)**, so this entry is history · Not built (batch H6) · Amends the contract's immediate
  `disable_shared_login`; carries out D98's item 4 and extends it · Source: `docs/mainnet-readiness.md` 1.14
- Decision: an owner turns shared login off through the existing `SetAllowShared {allow:false}`, so it waits the scope's
  `change_delay_ms`, and only while a Google client remains in the scope (an email client doesn't count). The change is
  checked at the proposal and again at execution. Hana Home shows a pending turn-off from `get_scope`.
- Options: (a) delay only; (b) keep it immediate; (c) delay and require a remaining Google client.
- Why (c): D98 had already chosen a delay, for D41's exit guarantee. `execute_change` already handles `allow:false`, so only
  the proposal's check changes and no state migrates. The client check closes a hole in the delay alone: `email:{scope}`
  counts in `scope.clients`, so a scope with shared login and email could otherwise end shared login with no Google client,
  stranding unlinked Google users.
- Limits: it stops a scope going email-only this way. The delay is at most 7 days and Hana never contacts users (D96),
  hence Home's notice. A partner loses its instant cut if Hana's login is compromised; Hana's pause remains.
- Not settled here: `remove_client` can still take the last Google client after a turn-off, because an email client
  satisfies its rule (`docs/hana-home-build-plan.md` "Still open", item 2).
- Contract change, no address impact.

- Note, 2026-11-09 (the user): `remove_client` can still remove the last Google client at once after a delayed turn-off; D468's exit client is the answer, so users keep access whatever the partner does.
### D461. Hana Home billing: a statement line while the app is active, Hana pays after it's gone

### D462. Hana Home lists apps from `scopes.first_session_at`
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** · Not built (batch H2) · Source:
  `docs/mainnet-readiness.md` 1.16
- Decision: Home's list is every scope with `scopes.first_session_at` set, and the wallet directory is a "your apps" overlay
  on it (D466).
- Options: (a) `session_markers`, as the readiness row proposed; (b) `scopes.first_session_at`; (c) the wallet directory only.
- Why (b) with (c) as an overlay: `session_markers` is written only while the scope's `first_session_at` is null, so later
  apps in a scope never get one. The directory is purged 30 days after a scope dies, exactly the shutdown case Home exists
  for. Home is keyed by scope anyway. It can over-list a scope whose first login failed, which is harmless.
- Amended 2026-11-09 (the owner's choice after H2's security review; exposure closed): the listing was per scope but its
  contents per app, so an unreleased app or staging origin in a scope with a login was visible to any Google account. Each app
  now has `apps.first_login_at` (migration 0016), written once on its first successful login, Google or email (`markFirstLogin`,
  only while the gate read it as null, so no write after the first; a failure is logged and the next login retries). Strangers
  see only apps with it set, in the list, a search, `?scopeId=` and `?appId=`, and a scope with none isn't listed at all. A link
  to an app with no login answers nothing to a stranger: nobody can have a wallet there. A scope's own users (`mine`) see all of
  its apps, marked or not, since the marker's write can fail and the directory is per scope, so it can't say which app they
  used. The backfill sets the earliest time proved by a session marker, a vault share, a user event, identity tokens or email
  sessions; any other app waits for its next successful login.

### D465. Remote sign-out stops auto-signing within about 10 s, in the vault's existing read
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** · Not built (batches H4, H5) · Amends D55 for auto-signing;
  sets the speed of D98's item 9 · "No new polling" amended by D680 (2026-11-10): every app's vault now reads its share about once a minute
- Decision: a revoked share stops auto-signing within about 10 s. It's checked in the vault's existing 10-second read
  (`GET /v1/app`, D62). No new polling.

## The test critical page (branch `feat/test-page-command`), 2026-11-09

### D449. The test critical page is sent by the deployed watchdog, behind its existing status token
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built: `apps/watchdog/src/test-page.ts`,
  `apps/watchdog/src/status.ts` (`GET`/`POST /test-page`), `scripts/lib/admin-test-page.ts` (`admin <env>
  watchdog:test-page [--yes]`); readiness 5.4 · Asked for by the user (readiness 5.4: a command that proves paging end to end)
- Context: the page must prove the path a real critical alert takes. The admin CLI is where such a command lives, but
  it can't send the page itself and prove that: the deployed Worker's secrets are not the local file (they can drift),
  and its network is not a laptop's (ntfy.sh rate-limited the Worker's shared IPs in the 2026-10-30 drill, HTTP 429s a
  laptop would never have seen).
- Decision: a new route on the watchdog. `GET /test-page` is the dry run (what the deployed Worker would use), `POST
  /test-page` sends one page on every critical channel with the same senders (`alerts.ts` `senderFor`, `sendSafe`). The
  command is `admin <env> watchdog:test-page`, a dry run without `--yes`, with the token from
  `.secrets/<env>/watchdog-secrets.json`. The route sits behind the existing bearer check (`WATCHDOG_STATUS_TOKEN`): an
  unauthenticated caller gets 401 and nothing happens; no token configured, 503.
- Why the existing token: its holders (the founders' secrets files and the admin Worker) can already acknowledge alerts,
  which is worse than ringing a phone with a page labelled TEST. A separate token would be one more secret to set and
  rotate for no gain. The admin Worker's client has no call to this route.
- Alternatives: (a) send from the operator's machine with the secrets file: no new route and no redeploy, but it proves
  neither the deployed secrets nor the Worker's network, the two things a drill most needs to catch. Not chosen.
  (b) a D1 flag the next cron run reads: no new cron needed, but no per-channel report back to the operator. (c) A real
  alert row through `deliverAlerts`: it would need acknowledging and re-send every 15 min (D450).
- Deploy: the watchdog redeployed once per env (no migration, new secret or var, no cron: 5 of 5 stay, D417); until then
  the command says the route is missing.

### D450. The test page is not an alert: no row, no dedupe, one send per 5 min, every channel reported as answered
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built: `apps/watchdog/src/test-page.ts`,
  `apps/watchdog/src/store.ts` (`claimTestPage`, `TEST_PAGE_META`) · Asked for by the user (it must not create an open
  alert or affect the dedupe)
- Decision:
  - No `alerts` or `deliveries` row, no alert kind, no dedupe key: nothing to acknowledge, no re-send, not in `/alerts`
    or the digest, and a real alert can't be suppressed by it. Its message id is negative, so PagerDuty's dedup key
    (`…-<alertId>`, ids from 1 up) can't equal a real alert's and a real alert never folds into a test incident. The
    record is the Worker's `test_page` log lines and the command's output.
  - Title `TEST (no action needed): paging check`, so `CRITICAL: TEST` is what a phone's lock screen shows; the body
    says nothing is wrong and how to quiet the paging app's own repeats. Pushover's 15-minute emergency repeats and
    PagerDuty's open incident stay, because they are part of what a critical page is.
  - One send per 5 min, claimed in one D1 statement before sending (`meta` key `test_page`): a leaked token or a loop
    can't ring phones at will, two racing requests send once, and it is short enough to fix a channel and retry.
  - Each channel as its provider answered; no credentials counts as failed; any failure exits non-zero; no retry (the
    real path retries every run, here a failure is the finding). "ok" means accepted: both founders confirming it
    arrived is the proof (`docs/operations.md` "Test page").
- Alternatives: a `test_page` alert kind acknowledged by hand: it needs a playbook, shows in the open-alerts list and
  re-sends until someone acts, all of which this must not do. No cooldown: one bad loop rings phones without limit.

### D468. A permanent exit client: the contract always accepts Hana Home's client, whatever a partner does
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09**; the mechanics are designed in batch H6 and reviewed there (`docs/hana-home-h6-design.md`, D480–D488; amended by D482 and D483 for who changes the list and how fast, D487 for the event)
- Context: access to a user's key depends on a client list the partner controls. D460's delay doesn't protect a user who
  isn't watching, because Hana doesn't contact users (D96), and after a delayed turn-off `remove_client` can still remove
  the last Google client at once. The user asked for a way for users to keep access to their funds whatever the partner does.
- Decision: the contract keeps a council-set list of exit clients (Hana Home's Google client and an email equivalent),
  changed only by the council under a timelock, and accepts them for every scope regardless of that scope's `clients` and
  `allow_shared`. A partner can't remove them or opt out. Each use emits an on-chain event the partner and the watchdog can
  see. It is a contract change in batch H6 and changes no path or key: Google's `sub` is the same across clients, so an
  exit client reaches the same wallet.
- Trade-offs: a compromised Hana Home page could reach users of every scope who sign in there, including partners who
  turned off shared login, so a partner can't fully exclude Hana. Hana still never holds a key: it takes the user's own
  sign-in, and the key exists only in their browser. Enterprises must be told (readiness 9.12); the external audit covers it.
- Rejected: a delay and a Home notice only (only helps users who look in time); pressing users to export or link a backup
  at signup (no guarantee); partner terms only (a legal remedy after the loss).
- Open for H6: whether D460's "needs a remaining Google client" and D464's owner seat are still needed once this exists. Settled 2026-11-09: neither is (D480, D481).
### D470. zod 3 → 4.6.7, with zod 3's error texts and `.url()` kept in one module
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built on `chore/zod-4` (`packages/env/src/zod.ts`,
  `packages/env/package.json`, `packages/console-core/package.json`, `apps/console/package.json`)
- Decision: `zod` `^4.6.6` (resolves to 4.6.7) in `packages/env`, `packages/console-core` and `apps/console`: the high-severity
  memory-exhaustion advisory GHSA-mrhx-c7xc-m3w5 is fixed only in 4.6.6. Every schema imports `z` from `@hana-id/env/zod`
  (new subpath), one module that keeps behaviour zod 4 would change: `z.config({customError})` maps every default message
  back to zod 3's words ("Required", "Unrecognized key(s) in object: …", "String must contain at least 1 character(s)", …),
  which reach partners through "Bad params for …" and every RPC refusal's `error`; `urlString()` replaces `.url()` (zod 4's
  trims and rewrites the value, and accepts a leading no-break space `new URL` refuses); `issuesAsZod3()` drops the follow-up
  issues zod 4 adds when one list is joined for a person. The `policy`, `params` and `json` keys of `z.unknown()` type are
  `.optional()`: zod 4 otherwise requires the key.
- Differences that remain, kept on purpose: an integer past 2^53 is refused by every `.int()` field (zod 3 let it through
  to whatever came next: those fields hold no value that large, and an unsafe integer is a bug to accept); `Infinity` is refused by `z.number()`
  without `.int()` (`usageRow` p50/p95, a staff audit detail number; `JSON.stringify` would store null). In a joined list
  the "Bad params" text no longer lists a range problem after "Expected integer, received float", and a value past 2^53 on
  a field with a smaller `.max()` names the safe-integer bound first. Neither first-issue text nor acceptance otherwise changes (checked by replaying
  138k generated inputs through every exported schema on both versions).
- Why: partner-visible words and accepted values shouldn't move with a dependency bump; zod's messages are a third party's
  wording, so they are pinned here, once. Rejected: (a) zod 4's new texts (partner-visible, no gain); (b) a message map at each
  safeParse site (six sites and every later one; misses operator CLI errors); (c) reimplementing `.int()` to allow unsafe
  integers (keeping an API bug).
- Out of scope: zod 3.22.4 and 3.25.76 stay in `apps/e2e`'s wallet-kit dev dependencies (`@reown/appkit-wallet` pins 3.22.4;
  `@coinbase/cdp-sdk`/viem peers want ^3), zod 4.6.5 in `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` (exact, dev): none is in `pnpm audit --prod`.

### D452. The npm token lives in a main-only GitHub environment; the job holding it runs none of the repo's code
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built on `fix/before-mainnet-sweep`
  (`.github/workflows/publish-sdk.yml`, `scripts/publish-gate.mjs`) · Security sweep OPER-4
- Decision: three jobs. `gate` (no environment) fails on a repository or organisation `NPM_TOKEN` and on an
  `npm-publish` environment not limited to exactly `main`, and skips while the environment doesn't exist. `build` runs
  install, tests and packing with no token and no OIDC. `publish`, on the environment, holds both, gated to `main` at the
  job level, and only downloads the tarballs and runs `npm publish`.
- Why: GitHub enforces an environment's deployment branches server-side, so a workflow edited on a branch can't reach
  the secret; a step's `if` can be edited away. Required reviewers aren't available on a private repository on GitHub
  Team (checked in GitHub's docs, 2026-11-09), so the branch rule is the control. Can't be run while CI is off and
  nothing is published; a misconfiguration fails closed.
- Alternatives: npm Trusted Publishing (no token; recommended once the repository or a public mirror exists, since
  npm generates provenance only from public repositories).

### D455. One relay per signed request across isolates, in the relayer key objects
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built on `fix/before-mainnet-sweep`
  (`apps/api/src/relayer-pool.ts` `claimKeyIndex`, `relayer-key.ts` `claims`) · Closes security.md (g)
- Decision: a session-signed request (derive, revoke, login, create session) goes through the relayer key its session
  key selects, with a claim of session key, session expiry and counter. The object holds a copy while the original is
  in flight, refuses it after a success (remembered 30 s, in memory) and relays it after a failure. Refused copies
  answer the endpoint's own 409, so clients see nothing new.
- Why: every copy has to meet in one place, and the relayer key object is already on each relay's path. Free-tier check
  (D417): no new Durable Object class, call, storage write or cron; replays stop costing transactions. Keys are still
  spread evenly, because session keys are random.
- Trade-offs: memory only, so an eviction or deploy forgets (the copy then fails on chain, the old cost); a change in
  the number of keys moves sessions between objects for that moment.
- Alternatives: (a) a Durable Object per session: an extra object call on every derive, for a cost of ~2.2 Tgas per
  copy. Not recommended. (b) the rate-limiter object's `reserve`, as `/v1/link*` does: an extra call and a storage
  write per relay. (c) D1: writes on the login path.
- Note (2026-11-09, independent review of `fix/before-mainnet-sweep`): two changes on `fix/before-mainnet-sweep-2`.
  **Failover.** A pure function of the session key meant a session on a bad key (out of allowance, deleted in a rotation,
  object unavailable) had no second chance: the vault's resend hit the same key. Now `relay()` retries a claimed relay
  once at `(keyIndex + 1) % count` with the same claim, for `near_rejected`, `near_unavailable`, `relayer_busy` and
  `relayer_unavailable` with no `nearTx`. Copies still meet, at the next object, because the next index depends only on
  the first. All but the last are "this transaction never ran": `near_rejected` is a definite rejection (a failed-over
  broadcast isn't; it's polled by hash, D435), `relayer_busy` a dropped or nonce-refused one, `near_unavailable` an RPC
  failure before sending. A thrown object
  call may have sent, but then the contract's check (session_key_in_use, or the counter) refuses the second transaction,
  at ~2.2 Tgas; if it isn't refused, the second is the first to land. When a first attempt that may have sent is followed
  by a definite failure, the client gets the first answer, so it polls instead of resending. A pool of one key doesn't
  fail over; revocation works through a bad key like any claimed relay. Cost: one extra object call on a failing relay.
  Limit: a copy reaching a recovered key after the original moved on is relayed again and fails on chain (the old cost).
  **Routing.** The first four bytes of a client-generated key let a client steer sessions to one index by grinding keys
  offline against a visible pool size. The index is now HMAC-SHA256 of the session key under the pool's secret
  (`RELAYER_KEYS`, the JSON value every isolate of a deploy has), with the label `hana-id-relayer-route-v1:<pool>`
  (`claimKeyIndex`), modulo the pool. Reusing that secret is sound here because it is API-only and always present
  (the optional `IDENTITY_SUB_KEY`/`USER_ID_KEY`/`VAULT_KEK` are not); HMAC-SHA256 under a distinct label doesn't relate
  to Ed25519's SHA-512 use of the seeds, and only the index mod N (a few bits) is observable. An upload of a changed
  `RELAYER_KEYS` reshuffles sessions between objects for a moment, like a change in the number of keys. A client now
  learns a session's key only after opening it; a session's own uses stay on one key (at most `MAX_USES`).

### D456. Each relayer pool holds only what an endpoint relays
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built on `fix/before-mainnet-sweep`
  (`apps/api/src/relayer-config.ts`, `gas.ts`, `scripts/lib/contract.ts`, the sandbox tests) · Closes security.md (h)
- Decision: `prune_sessions` leaves the session pool; `register_scope` and `apply_pending_config` leave the owner pool,
  with their gas entries and `register_scope`'s per-proof gas. `prune_sessions` and `apply_pending_config` can be called
  by anyone from their own account. If public registration ever opens, `register_scope` returns with its own review
  (`docs/contract-interface.md` already says the API must not relay it while a sponsor pays its storage).
- Why now: it had been folded into batch B's allowlist step, which never ran and can't while `/v1/sessions` remains the
  vault's fallback; a mainnet env gets the narrow keys from its first deploy at no cost.
- Cost: on sandbox-dev, once: the relayer keys are deleted and re-added, a short outage of logins there
  (`docs/operations.md` "Narrowing the relayer keys"). Batch B's state 2 and 3 are still open and are not decided here.
- Note (2026-11-09, independent review of `fix/before-mainnet-sweep`; `fix/before-mainnet-sweep-2`): the outage is gone.
  `deploy-contract`'s `relayer-keys` step now swaps each wrong-permission key in place: one transaction per pool on the
  relayer account, `DeleteKey` then `AddKey` of the same public key, so no key is ever missing and a failed transaction
  changes nothing (near-sandbox test `access_keys_a_relayer_key_is_swapped_in_one_transaction`). A full-access key in a
  pool file stays a blocker: the plan never deletes one. The narrowing runbook is now a single `deploy-contract --yes`.
  A swapped or re-added key restarts at a nonce on a whole multiple of 10^6 (NEAR's AddKey), so the admin's nonce check
  now takes such a nonce with no ledger row as a new baseline (`rebaselined`), explained and not `nonce_unexplained`: the
  review's false alert. Residual: a holder of a leaked key could deliberately aim one last transaction at such a nonce to
  pass this check, at the cost of allowance the watchdog watches (`docs/security.md`, the nonce check).

### D457. `deploy-contract` names unknown full-access keys and takes only reproducible builds outside dev envs
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built on `fix/before-mainnet-sweep`
  (`scripts/lib/deploy-plan.ts`, `deploy-run.ts`) · Security sweep OPER-7
- Decision: a full-access key other than the local keychain key on the relayer, an owner account or a dev env's signer,
  and any on the council DAO: a warning in dev envs, a blocker elsewhere (no local key to compare: a warning). Outside
  dev envs a build step or a proposal of `target/`'s wasm is refused, so new code comes only from `--wasm` (D86);
  executing an already proposed hash is allowed. A first deploy compares the code hash on chain with the wasm it sent.
- Why: a forgotten full-access key or a swapped wasm replaces the contract, and with it every user's keys. Warnings in
  dev envs, because sandbox-dev may legitimately hold extra keys.
- Note (2026-11-09, independent review of `fix/before-mainnet-sweep`; `fix/before-mainnet-sweep-2`): "takes only
  reproducible builds" overstated what the check was: it only tested that `--wasm` was passed. Outside dev envs a
  `propose-upgrade` or `deploy` step now also needs the wasm's code hash in `CONTRACT_RELEASES` (`packages/console-core`):
  named by file, published first. It can't prove the file was built reproducibly (that is the release process, D86), so
  the blocker now says "a published build".

### D471. After an answer the approval popup says what the answer did, and counts down its real time left
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: asked for by the user (the screen and its request wording), the consent wording and the
  Close now guard confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built on `fix/approval-waiting-screen` (`packages/web/src/auth/approve-page.ts`
  `answeredView`, `idleClose`; `auth.css`) · Number note: the next free number above D470 on `origin/develop`; renumber
  at the merge if another branch took it
- Decision: the screen that said "Done / Waiting for the next request from {app}…" for the popup's 15 s reuse
  (unchanged, as is the queue) now says, by kind of answer: an approved request **Approved** with a check mark, "You can go
  back to {App}." and "If it needs another approval, it’ll appear here."; a rejected request **Declined** and "Nothing
  was signed."; an allowed consent **Allowed** with the same two lines; a refused consent **Not allowed** and "Automatic
  signing wasn’t turned on.". Under each: "Closing in N s" and **Close now**.
- Why: "Done" was inaccurate (the request is approved; the transaction may not be sent), and the waiting line didn't
  say the window would close. A consent signs nothing, so "Approved" and "Nothing was signed" don't fit it, and "Not
  allowed" says what actually happened: the vault records the refusal and automatic signing stays off.
- The countdown: one deadline, set where `idleClose` schedules the close, and only `answer()` shows it. The text is
  read from that deadline at each whole second (a throttled background window can't make it wrong) and cleared with
  the idle timer by a new request, a close and `hana:approve-close`. The loading screens' `idleClose` (15 s on a
  vault-opened popup, 8 s on a partner-opened one) show none: nothing is promised there. It isn't a live region (the
  result above it is), and nothing animates.
- Close now takes the timer's path (`byeAndClose`: `hana:approve-bye`, then close), so the vault stops reusing the
  window. It ignores clicks in the screen's first 1 s (`GUARD_DELAY_MS`, as D36) so the rest of a double-click on
  Approve or Reject can't close the window and cost the follow-up, and the page never focuses it. In the 420 × 680
  popup it sits well above where Approve and Reject were (checked in `tests/approval.spec.ts`); the 1 s covers a short
  or scrolled window.
- Alternatives: (a) the full Approve guard on Close now (an arming gesture, then a press after it): one more tap for
  a touch user on a button that can sign nothing; the guard exists for signing. Not done. (b) A button that stays
  disabled for the 1 s: a flash of a disabled style on every answer, for a click nobody means to make. Not done. (c) An
  `aria-live` countdown: read out every second. Not done.

## Hana Home H1: the identity (branch `feat/hana-home-h1`), 2026-11-09

### D473. Hana Home's identity verifier: what is signed, and how refusals answer
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built: `packages/core/src/home.ts`,
  `apps/api/src/home/identity.ts`, `apps/api/src/log.ts`, `apps/api/src/http.ts` `readBody`,
  `apps/api/src/login-token.ts` (`appId` absent only with `anyLoginMethod: true`) · Implements `docs/hana-home-spec.md`
  "Identity without a user database" (D98, D463) · Reviewed 2026-11-09 by batch H1's independent security review: no
  critical, high or medium issue; one low cost issue (D475), one test gap (the signed vector now goes through
  `homeGate` and is asserted in core), and conditions on later batches (`docs/hana-home-build-plan.md`, `docs/security.md`)
- Decision:
  - The signed `path` is the URL's path **and query** (`homeRequestPath`). The spec said only "path"; a query like
    `/v1/home/devices?scopeId=` must not be changeable under the signature, and both ends take it from `URL`.
  - `x-hana-home` is strict (exactly six fields, canonical base64url, `salt` exactly 32 bytes, at most 12 288 characters).
    A session's salt is 16–64 bytes; Home has no reason to vary.
  - `homeGate` runs the spec's order, plus a per-IP limit right after the origin and a per-Home-key limit after the
    signature and before the single-use mark, so a refused request doesn't spend its counter.
  - Every credential refusal is 401, the page's "sign in again" (the spec's Expiry section), whatever `verifyLoginToken`
    would answer on a login (`token_expired` is 400 there). Except: `409 counter_reused`, 429 limits, and outages stay 5xx
    with the codes logins use. A refusal never carries `verifyLoginToken`'s `data`.
  - The key-lead-time observer (`keyObserver`) is not passed: a Home identity is verified on every call, and D422's
    last-token sighting concerns on-chain use, which H3's derive records for itself.
  - `log()` drops the field names `x-hana-home`, `sub`, `pathHash`, `path_hash`, `jwt`, `token`, `idToken`, `id_token` at
    runtime, wherever nested, as a backstop to `LogFields`' compile-time allow-list.
- Why: the plan's H1 and the spec's check order; 10 ms CPU and 50 subrequests (D417): at most three limiter calls, two
  chain reads and three JWKS/key reads (cached), all native crypto.
- Limits: a retired shared client's token keeps passing for up to 60 s, the per-isolate `get_config` cache; a fresh read
  on every call would cost a subrequest for that window. No route calls the gate until H2.
- Address impact: none. No path, tuple or key rule changes.

### D474. The email issuer's Home audience is `hana-home`; one function decides which clients make a Home identity
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built: `HOME_EMAIL_AUDIENCE`
  (`packages/core/src/home.ts`), `homeAudienceRoute` (`apps/api/src/home/identity.ts`) · For D463 and D468
- Decision: the audience of a Home identity's email token is the constant `hana-home`, meant to be on no scope. It isn't
  `email:`-prefixed, and the issuer's client-proof route mints only for `email:{scope}`. That alone is **not yet a
  guarantee** (H1's review, 2026-11-09): `propose_change`'s `AddClient` checks a client proof's provider, `aud` and nonce
  and nothing about the `aud`'s form (`registry.rs`), so once H10's route signs `hana-home` over a caller-supplied nonce,
  an owner could put `client_proof_nonce` in it for their own mailbox and register `("email", "hana-home")` on their
  scope. Today nothing signs `hana-home`, so nothing can register it. H6 or H10 must refuse that client (the build
  plan's H10); until then "on no scope" holds only because the route doesn't exist. H10's issuer route signs it and
  imports the constant; each env's tokens are already bound by `iss` and keys, so it needs no env-specific value.
  `homeAudienceRoute` is the single place that says which clients are accepted (shared Google in force, this audience,
  never a scope client). H6 adds the exit client (D468) there and in the `get_config` read, nothing else: the gate, the
  nonce, the header and the routes above it don't change.
- Options: an env-specific audience (no gain over `iss`); registering a real on-chain client for Home (it could then be
  claimed or removed through the registry, which spec item 14 avoids).
- Open for H6: whether Home signs in through the exit client instead of the first shared client, which would add a field to
  `/v1/home/config` (`sharedGoogleClientId` stays). Settled 2026-11-09: Home signs in through a dedicated exit client (D484).
- Note, 2026-11-09 (H6's security review): the email route is no longer by audience alone. `homeAudienceRoute` also requires
  `("email", "hana-home")` in force on the exit list (D494 point 5), so D483's emergency removal covers email. An older contract
  or an empty list refuses it, as they refuse Google's exit client.

### D475. A limiter call's row reads don't depend on how many single-use markers the object holds
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: decided while building, confirmed by the user 2026-11-09 · Built: `apps/api/src/rate-limiter.ts` (`reserve`,
  `scheduleMarkerSweep`, `prune`), `apps/api/test/rate-limiter-marks.test.ts` · H1's independent security review (low,
  cost) · Address impact: none
- Decision: `reserve` no longer sweeps expired markers on each call; the object's alarm deletes them. `prune` lists only
  the keys of the limits being hit (prefix `<name>@`), not every key. `homeGate`'s per-key limit and counter now read
  about three rows on the Home key's object however many markers it holds, where they read about two per marker: enough
  for one identity to spend a large share of the free tier's Durable Object row reads (D417) and fail every limiter
  closed.
- The alarm had to change too: `scheduleMarkerSweep` used to move an armed alarm out to each new marker's end, which on a
  shared object with steady traffic (`owner-actions:tokens`, `link-tokens`) never fires, and the per-call sweep was what
  was really cleaning those objects. The alarm is now armed only when none is armed, and it re-arms itself for the
  latest live marker. An expired marker is gone within one further marker lifetime (at most the longest the object sees:
  an owner token's `exp`, 10 min for a link claim, 20 min for a Home counter), and each marker is read at most a couple of
  times in all.
- Unchanged: a marker is refused while live and free from exactly `untilMs`, whether or not it has been swept; `release`;
  `hit`'s windows and refusals; every caller of `reserve` (owner and step-up tokens, identity proofs, link claims, mainnet
  demo proofs, Home counters).
- Options: a `limit` on the sweep (still a cost per call, and a sweep that can fall behind for good); Home's markers in
  their own object (fixes Home only, and adds a limiter call).

## Sodax's USDC bridge in the mainnet demo (branch `feat/mainnet-demo-usdc-bridge`), 2026-11-09

### D476. The sandbox mainnet demo signs Sodax's USDC ⇄ USDC bridge between Base and Stellar, delivered to the user's own wallet
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: asked for by the user 2026-11-09 (the bridge in the sample's mainnet demo, and the recipient binding "if the vault can check that simply"); the security review of 2026-11-09 found one High, fixed on `feat/mainnet-demo-usdc-bridge-2` (below) · Built on `feat/mainnet-demo-usdc-bridge` and `feat/mainnet-demo-usdc-bridge-2`, not merged, not deployed (`packages/core/src/mainnet-demo.ts` `checkSodaxHubCalls`, `checkBridgeCalls`, `checkBridgeHubWallet`, `sodaxHubWallet`, `bridgeRecipient`; `packages/web/src/vault/signing.ts`, `vault.ts`; `packages/web/src/auth/approve-page.ts`) · Number note: was D475 on the branch; renumbered when `develop` took D475 for the limiter · Amends D429 point 3, with a row of "Superseded or amended".
- The problem: every bridge was refused (`mainnet_demo_unknown_call`) because a deposit's hub calls had to be empty or exactly two. Sodax's bridge (`@sodax/sdk` 2.2.0 `buildBridgeData`, no partner fee) is four calls. Base USDC and Stellar USDC are the only demo pair sharing a vault (sodaUSDC); EURC is two separate hub assets and never bridges, and Base ETH's Stellar counterpart isn't a demo token.
- Decision: a Sodax deposit's hub calls may also be exactly:
  1. on srcHub, `approve(sodaUSDC, amount)`;
  2. on sodaUSDC, `deposit(srcHub, amount)`;
  3. on sodaUSDC, `withdraw(dstHub, amount × 10^(18−srcDec))`;
  4. on the hub asset manager, `transfer(dstHub, recipient, delivered, 0x)`.
- The rules: srcHub is the deposited asset's own hub asset and dstHub the other of the pinned pair (`0x72E8…259C` Base USDC, 6 decimals; `0x3480…40f2` Stellar USDC, 7 decimals), so EURC, ETH and XLM are refused; sodaUSDC `0xAbbb…A833` and the hub asset manager `0x60c5…37C0` are pinned; every amount is an exact equality, not ≤ (approve = deposit = amount, withdraw = amount × 10^(18−srcDec), delivered × 10^(18−dstDec) = withdraw); every `value` is 0 and the transfer's `data` empty; exactly four calls (a partner-fee call makes five and is refused). The exact equality also means dust is refused: a Stellar amount that isn't a whole number of 6-decimal units (1.0000001 USDC, which the SDK would floor) doesn't pass, and neither does a zero amount. Valuation, the $9.99 cap and the spoke and auth checks are unchanged: the deposit is what is valued.
- The recipient is bound (the user's "if the vault can check that simply"): it was simple, since the vault holds both session addresses at signing. `assessMainnetDemo` takes `{ wallets: { evm, stellar } }` (the vault, and the usage report); the recipient must be canonical for the destination (20 bytes for Base; 44 bytes for Stellar, the SCV_ADDRESS XDR with the account prefix `00000012` `00000000` `00000000`) and equal to the session's own address on that chain, compared in the encoded form the hub receives. A wrong recipient is refused before any popup (`mainnet_demo_unknown_call`). What the binding does not do: it constrains a request of the bridge's shape only. A page can still move up to the cap elsewhere with a plain send, or a Sodax swap or plain deposit whose spoke `to` is another hub wallet (D429, the spec's R5); those are capped and shown, and unchanged here.
- The hub wallet is bound (the High from the independent security review of 2026-11-09, verified on the branch and fixed there): the deposit's spoke `to` is where the funds reach the hub first, and it was discarded, so a compromised page on the allowed app could build a correct bridge with the user's own recipient and set `to` to another hub wallet. `checkBridgeCalls` now requires `to` to be exactly the signing address's own hub wallet (20 bytes), in both directions and in both modes, `{ wallets }` and `'shown'`: the signing address is all the derivation needs, so the popup checks it too, and the vault refuses a wrong `to` before any popup (`mainnet_demo_unknown_call`). The wallet is computed offline, with no new network read at signing (`sodaxHubWallet`, `sodaxHubWalletOf`): salt = keccak256(factory ‖ relayChainId as a 32-byte word ‖ user), proxy = the last 20 bytes of keccak256(0xff ‖ factory ‖ salt ‖ `21c35dbe…7c1f`, the CREATE3 proxy's init-code hash), wallet = the last 20 bytes of keccak256(0xd694 ‖ proxy ‖ 0x01). Factory `0xA0ed3047D358648F2C0583B415CffCA571FDB544`, relay id 30 for Base with the 20-byte address, 27 for Stellar with the 44-byte SCV_ADDRESS XDR. Read from the factory's bytecode (`eth_getCode` on the proxy and on its EIP-1967 implementation `0x0b45be992010f95d428c03cc67751827ed65cf9a`, through `rpc.soniclabs.com`, 2026-11-09) and confirmed against five answers of the factory's own `getDeployedAddress` (read-only `eth_call`), pinned as test vectors in `packages/core/test/mainnet-demo.test.ts`. The swap path had the same gap (R5), since closed by D492: the check moved to `checkSodaxHubCalls` (`checkSpokeHubWallet`, was `checkBridgeHubWallet`) and covers every deposit. The hostile harness now refuses every byte of `to` and its length word, an empty `to`, a wrong length, another user's hub wallet and the wrong chain's relay id, in both directions.
- The popup: below the value line, `Bridge 1 USDC from Base to Stellar, 1:1. Recipient on Stellar: G…`, from the popup's own decoding of the bytes (the same function as the vault's, read-only `'shown'` recipients: the popup holds the signing chain's address only, so it shows the recipient rather than binding it; the vault binds it before the popup opens). The popup does check the spoke `to` against the signing address, so it names a recipient only once the hub wallet is verified; otherwise it shows the cap line alone. Omitting the argument refuses a bridge, so no caller can skip it silently. No protocol change: `hana:approve-request` validates its keys exactly, so a new field would break an older popup. An older popup can't value a bridge: it shows only the cap line (`Hana's limit is $9.99 per transaction.`), with neither the value nor the bridge line, and an approval there is still possible, as for any request it can't value. An older vault refuses bridges as before, and no SDK changes.
- Risks accepted for the demo:
  - **Stuck funds**: a bridge has no solver refund path, and where a failure leaves the funds depends on where it happens. Bounded by the $9.99 cap per transaction.
    - A hub revert (for example no destination liquidity at the vault's withdraw) leaves the funds in the user's hub wallet, where key export applies: `sodax.recovery.withdrawHubAsset` (`sendMessage` to the connection contract) is refused by the classifier. This rests on the hub wallet running the four calls atomically, which is the SDK's comment and has not been verified against the contracts or on chain.
    - A missing Stellar trustline or an unfunded destination account fails after the hub transfer, so the funds have left the hub wallet and key export likely can't help. Recovery depends on Sodax re-delivering, which is unconfirmed.
    - Only the sample page blocks a missing trustline. The vault doesn't check the destination account.
  - **Pins fail closed**: if Sodax redeploys sodaUSDC, the hub asset manager or a hub asset, every bridge is refused until the pins are reviewed and rebuilt.
  - **Vault fees**: `tokenInfo` has `depositFee`/`withdrawalFee`, which the SDK ignores. Read live on 2026-11-09 from sodaUSDC through `rpc.soniclabs.com` (read-only `eth_call`), both zero: Base USDC's hub asset `0x72E8…259C` decimals 6, depositFee 0, withdrawalFee 0, maxDeposit 100000000000, isSupported true; Stellar USDC's `0x3480…40f2` decimals 7, depositFee 0, withdrawalFee 0, maxDeposit 1500000000000, isSupported true. A fee can change after this read, so read both again before enabling the bridge. A non-zero fee would break the SDK's fixed amounts: the bridge would revert and strand the funds, or draw that fee from earlier sodaUSDC or destination hub-asset balance.
  - The exact bytes and pins come from packaged `@sodax/sdk` 2.2.0 and offline encoders; nothing was run against Sodax's API (blocked), and the only live reads are the factory's and sodaUSDC's above (`eth_call`, `eth_getCode`, `eth_getStorageAt`), through Sonic's public RPC.
  - **The factory is upgradeable**: a UUPS proxy (`upgradeToAndCall`, owner-only, two-step ownership) over implementation `0x0b45be992010f95d428c03cc67751827ed65cf9a` on 2026-11-09. The offline formula is what that implementation computes, so an upgrade that changes it makes the SDK's `to` stop matching and every bridge is refused until the formula is reviewed and rebuilt (fail closed; a stuck bridge can't result, since nothing is signed). The check proves the address, not the wallet's code: what the hub wallet does with funds remains trust in Sodax's contracts. To read again before enabling, with the fees: the implementation slot and the five vectors.
- Why this and not: (a) `≤` instead of `=` (it would let a call spend less and strand or reroute value): not done. (b) The popup binding the recipient: it would need a new field in `hana:approve-request`, which older popups reject; the vault is the authority and already refuses, and the popup shows what the bytes say. Not done. (c) A new `bridge` movement kind: the value and cap are unchanged, so it would add nothing to the vault's decision; the popup's description is carried beside the movements instead. Not done.
## Hana Home H6: the exit client's design (branch `docs/hana-home-h6-design`), 2026-11-09

Decided by the user on the review of H6's design (`docs/hana-home-h6-design.md`, which holds the code references and the
tests). Not built. None changes a path, a key or derivation: `aud` never enters the path, `ik`, `settle` or
`path_identity`, so every wallet keeps its address.

### D480. Turning off shared login stays immediate and needs no remaining Google client (D460 dropped)
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** · Reverses the user's D460 and D98's item 4 · Source:
  `docs/hana-home-h6-design.md` section 3
- Decision: D460 is dropped. `disable_shared_login` keeps working unchanged (neither removed nor a stub), turning shared
  login off stays immediate, and it needs no remaining Google client. `remove_client` of the last Google client keeps
  today's rule.
- Options: (a) keep D460 (the scope's delay, a remaining Google client); (b) drop it.
- Why (b): the exit client (D468) covers users, so the delay no longer protects anyone, and a delayed turn-off would break
  an existing defence: owners answer a new shared client by turning shared login off first, and a delay of the same length
  can't land first.
- Falls away: the delayed turn-off, Home's notice of a pending turn-off, the caller changes (`validate.ts`,
  `SAFETY_METHODS`, the console) and the partner notice.

### D481. Hana holds no owner seat on partner scopes (D464's seat dropped)
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** · Drops D464; D98's item 3 no longer needs a right to enable
  shared login at exit · Source: `docs/hana-home-h6-design.md` section 3
- Decision: D464's Hana owner seat is dropped. Hana has no owner rights over partner scopes. D464's note that the Hana
  council would hold the seat stays only as history.
- Options: (a) keep the seat; (b) drop it.
- Why (b): the seat's only purpose was proposing `SetAllowShared` at exit, which the exit client now makes unnecessary.
  Keeping it would leave Hana with `SetOwners` and `AddClient` proposal rights over partner scopes for no gain.
- Consequences: the build plan's open item 6 closes; readiness 9.11 closes, because there is nothing to word.

### D482. A new exit client waits the upgrade delay
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** · Not built (batch H6) · Source: `docs/hana-home-h6-design.md`
  section 1
- Decision: a new exit client comes into force only after `governance_delay_ms` (72 h on mainnet), through
  `set_exit_clients`.
- Options: (a) the scope delay (`change_delay_ms`, at most 7 days); (b) the upgrade delay.
- Why (b): an exit client reaches every scope, including those that refused shared login. That is close to the power of an
  upgrade, so it gets the upgrade's delay.

### D483. An exit client can be removed at once by the council and is then retired forever
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** · Not built (batch H6) · Amends D468's "under a timelock",
  for removals only · Source: `docs/hana-home-h6-design.md` section 1
- Decision: the council can remove an exit client immediately. A removed client is retired forever (an `#exit` marker, as
  `RETIRED_SHARED`), so it can never be claimed again.
- Options: (a) immediate; (b) under the timelock, as D468's wording had it.
- Why (a): it is the only way to stop a compromised Home without pausing every partner, and a removal can't steal
  anything.

### D484. The exit uses a new, dedicated Google client, in the same Google Cloud project as the shared client
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** (the reason below is the user's correction of the design's) ·
  Not built (batch H6) · Settles D474's open point for H6 · Source: `docs/hana-home-h6-design.md` section 1
- Decision: the exit uses a new, dedicated Google client in the same Google Cloud project as the shared client. Its only
  redirect can be Home's page.
- Options: (a) a new, dedicated client; (b) reuse the shared client.
- Why (a), precisely: a dedicated client adds no security boundary on Google's side and doesn't defend against a
  compromised Hana page. It exists so the contract can tell an exit from a normal login, by `aud`: partners' turning off
  shared login keeps meaning something, and the session limits (D486), the alert counter (D487) and the emergency removal
  (D483) apply to exits only.
- Condition: that Google's `sub` is the same across clients is Google's behaviour, not this code's. It must be confirmed
  live with the real client before use (one spike with two accounts is the only evidence so far, `docs/context.md`).

### D485. The email exit reaches scopes that dropped their email client
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** · Not built (batches H6, H10) · As D468 · Source:
  `docs/hana-home-h6-design.md` sections 1, 4
- Decision: the email exit (`("email", "hana-home")`) reaches every registered scope, as D468 says, including scopes that
  dropped their email client. A stolen email signing key therefore reaches further than it does today, and that is
  accepted. A second signer for the email issuer is a priority (readiness 2.5a).
- Options: (a) reach those scopes; (b) a Google-only exit.
- Why (a): a user who signed in with email can hold funds in a scope whose owner later drops the email client, and D468
  promises those users an exit too. The defence against a stolen key is its custody and a second signer (D121).
- Note, 2026-11-10 (H10's security review, D667, confirmed by the user 2026-11-10): the email exit reaches **any** registered scope, including one
  that never had an email client. What stops a code opening a wallet where the user had none is D544's `home_no_wallet`
  (no derive for an identity the chain shows never opened a wallet there), and it applies only where links are open.

### D486. Exit sessions: at most 30 minutes and 3 uses on chain; `link_jwt` refused
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** · Not built (batch H6) · Source:
  `docs/hana-home-h6-design.md` section 2
- Decision: the contract limits an exit session to 30 minutes and 3 uses, and refuses `link_jwt` on it.
- Options: (a) these limits; (b) none.
- Why (a): they stop exit becoming a general login route, and 2 or more uses are needed to retry an MPC failure. They don't
  stop a compromised page.

### D487. An hourly on-chain exit counter that alerts and never refuses; one event per session
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** · Not built (batch H6) · Reads D468's "each use" as each
  session · Source: `docs/hana-home-h6-design.md` section 2
- Decision: `get_config` exposes an hourly exit total for the watchdog. It alerts and never refuses. The contract emits one
  event per exit session, carrying no `sub`.
- Options: (a) an on-chain counter; (b) partners' indexers only.
- Why (a): the watchdog reads views, not logs. It never refuses, as D200 reasoned, because a refusing cap could be burned
  to lock users out of their rescue route. One event per session, because later derives in it release the same key. No new
  RPC or cron (D380, D417).

### D488. No waiting period before an exit releases a key
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09** · Source: `docs/hana-home-h6-design.md` section 4
- Decision: an exit releases the key with no waiting period.
- Options: (a) a delay on exit derives; (b) none.
- Why (b): a delay would cover only scopes with shared login off, needs a marker on every session and a two-visit Home flow,
  and would slow the rescue exactly when it's needed. The only real gain, time for a mass-harvest alarm, comes mostly from
  the counter (D487), without touching real users.

### D489. Enterprise partners are told plainly they can't exclude Hana Home; legal reviews "keep clients 2 years"

### D490. Hana Home uses the exit client only where a scope's normal route is gone
- Date 2026-11-09 · Status: **decided by the user 2026-11-09**
